title: In the Short Term, AI Is a Complexity Machine, Not an Efficiency Tool
dek: AI lets everyone write and do research, and the result is more emails, more decks, more decisions. Jim VandeHei says that in the short term it manufactures complexity, and only deliberate deletion gets your time back.
why: Medium information density, but the "confront, delete, amplify" framework and the hands-on details of the health AI agent Axios built for itself are worth hearing.
who: For founders and managers bringing AI into their organizations, and for anyone crushed by the information overload AI brings and wanting to reclaim their time.
skip: The opening section on the midterms and the political toxicity of data centers has little to do with the AI efficiency theme.

points.h: A six-month plan is already a fantasy
points.body: Jim says he used to mock one-, two-, three-year plans, and now even a six-month plan seems laughable to him — he can only have high confidence in things six to seven weeks out. He gives a concrete number: six months ago, 30% to 40% of Axios traffic came from Google Search; now it has fallen to 5% to 10%, involving millions of users, and it happened almost overnight. He calls this state post-processable velocity: the AI world is moving faster than humans can understand it. This is not abstract anxiety; it is a traffic structure rewritten within months.

points.h: Most companies are stuck in the messy middle
points.body: Jim calls the current phase the messy middle: companies start using AI, build prototypes, see the promise, and then discover "I have to connect it to my data pool," which is far harder than expected. He describes a split: people in Silicon Valley feel it is 1999 and everything is about to explode; but most people in Toledo, Topeka, Oshkosh feel "I'm just running my company, AI is probably that new thing, employees are talking about it, we'll use it eventually." Introducing any technology into an existing company is hard, because you have to connect it to the clunky systems built over the past decade.

points.h: In the short term, AI is a complexity creation machine
points.body: Jim says flatly that for most people in the short term, AI is a complexity creation machine. The mechanism: now anyone can use AI to write something decent, anyone can do deep research and dump it into an email to their boss. The result is that everyone receives more emails, more decks, more ideas — some well thought out, many not. So it's "oh God, now I have more decisions to make." This is exactly why he wrote the book: how to help you delete the things you do out of habit and inertia, so you can amplify what you actually want to do.

points.h: The 25% wasted each week is habit, not ability
points.body: Jim cites data from The Economist and others: on average, 25% of each week is spent on things that shouldn't be done or have no value to the company, because of habit and inertia. He does the math: 25% means two and a half years wasted out of every decade. He stresses that AI will not solve this now — "I thought AI would make us more efficient, and right now it isn't." In the short term people are anxious and confused, and he thinks you should be anxious and confused, because this is a strange time to be alive.

points.h: First confront, then delete, and only then amplify
points.body: The framework has three steps: confront is the psychological move, asking "why am I doing this" and "does this meeting really need to happen"; delete is cutting it or saying no; amplify is doing what you're good at, what you like, what brings promotion or reward. Jim says this system has been running at Axios for two or three years, and the effect is that people are more focused, more productive, but most importantly happier. He gives the example of the "let's kill shit" meeting: bring the leadership team together, spend an hour or two listing all the stupid meetings, processes, and products, and then kill them. That's how the Axios app got cut — tens of millions of people come to Axios, but only 30,000 use the app regularly, while maintenance costs are extremely high.

points.h: Make more decisions and your decision-making gets worse
points.body: Jim says the average person receives about 120 texts and 150 emails a day, and this mental strain is underestimated. He cites brain scan research: the more decisions you make, the worse your decision-making becomes, and this is called cognitive fatigue. So unless you reduce the number of decisions you have to make, you won't perform well on the decisions you actually want to make. He gives a personal example: setting recurring purchases like toothpaste and deodorant to Amazon auto-order, so he never has to think about them again. These small things add up to fewer decisions and more time, which is what lets you read books and have coffee with people.

points.h: AI won't replace journalists, it will replace the generic consultant
points.body: Jim says he doesn't think AI will replace journalists, nor most jobs. He names one that will be replaced: the generic consultant — AI is already decent at general consulting and business analysis. But for anyone with passion, as long as they can treat this technology as a force multiplier for their specific work and get very fluent with it, they'll be fine, even more in demand. He judges that fluency with AI will soon become table stakes in the workplace. This is also the logic behind Axios Local's expansion: use AI for distribution, copy editing, and other back-end work that isn't core to journalism, drive costs down, and then hire hundreds of reporters.

points.h: Never bet your business model on a third party's goodwill
points.body: Axios has a content licensing deal with OpenAI. Jim's logic is direct: ChatGPT, Google, and Anthropic have already eaten all the public information on the internet, including everything Axios has ever written. So there are only two paths — sue like The New York Times and hope to win, or accept the licensing fee. He judges that Axios can't win a lawsuit, and its content volume isn't large enough that even a win would be worth the damages. He stresses the difference from BuzzFeed betting on Facebook: this revenue could disappear tomorrow and the company's overall performance wouldn't be affected. His principle: never bet your business model on the generosity of a third party that has no vested interest in your business.

points.h: The Claude project he built for his wife beats doctors
points.body: Jim built a project for his wife in Claude: input all her health information, specify that the AI only pull from sources like Johns Hopkins and Mayo, have it review new medical literature every two weeks, and cross-reference online with people who have similar symptoms. He says it was better than any doctor he had seen, until they finally went to Mayo and met a doctor who could approach the level of this system. His own use is to feed all his blood tests, MRIs, and family history into ChatGPT. He admits he has a concierge doctor and takes the results to be checked, and the doctor says every time "this is pretty good," and one doctor now uses this setup for most of his work.

quotes.text: I've always laughed at like year or two or three-year planning. I'm like, how the hell do you do that? But now I kind of laugh at six-month planning.
I think for most people in the short term, it is a complexity creation machine.
Well, think of a 25%, man. That's two and a half years out of every decade that I pissed away doing things I don't want to do or shouldn't be doing.
There's been tons of studies, tons of brain scans that show the more decisions that you make, the worse you get at making decisions. It's called cognitive fatigue, mental fatigue.
don't ever bet your model on the generosity of a third party that has no vested stake in your business.
